reasoning: Rules from p-05: Na/K = +1, Ca = +2, Al = +3, O = -2 (except peroxides = -1), H = +1 (hydridic = -1 when H is bonded to a less electronegative element), sum = 0 for a neutral compound. (a) +1 +2(+1) + P + 4(-2) = 0 -> P = +5. (b) +1 +1 + S -8 = 0 -> S = +6. (c) 4(+1) + 2P + 7(-2) = 0 -> 2P = 10 -> P = +5. (d) 2(+1) + Mn + 4(-2) = 0 -> Mn = +6. (e) CaO2 is calcium PEROXIDE, not a normal oxide: Ca is an alkaline-earth metal so Ca = +2 by rule 2, hence the two oxygens must total -2 and each O = -1 (exactly the peroxide exception on p-05). (f) NaBH4: electronegativity B 2.04 < H 2.20, so hydrogen is hydridic, H = -1: +1 + B + 4(-1) = 0 -> B = +3. (The alternative H = +1 would give B = -5, impossible for a group-13 element whose highest state is +3.) (g) H2S2O7 (pyrosulphuric acid) has NO O-O linkage, so every O = -2: 2(+1) + 2S + 7(-2) = 0 -> 2S = 12 -> S = +6. (h) Potash alum: K = +1, Al = +3, so the two sulphate groups carry -4 in total, i.e. each SO4 is -2; within SO4(2-), S + 4(-2) = -2 -> S = +6. The 12 H2O of crystallisation are neutral and do not enter.

answer: (a) KI3: I = -1/3 (average). Reality: K+[I-I-I]- is I2 coordinated to I-, so two iodines are 0 and one is -1; average -1/3.  (b) H2S4O6: S = +2.5 (average). Reality (chapter's own S4O6(2-) structure, p-10): the two terminal S are +5 and the two middle S are 0; average = (5+0+0+5)/4 = +2.5.  (c) Fe3O4: Fe = +8/3 (average). Reality: a MIXED oxide FeO.Fe2O3, i.e. one Fe(II) and two Fe(III); average = (2+3+3)/3 = 8/3.  (d) CH3CH2OH - BOTH carbons underlined: C of CH3 = -3, C of CH2OH = -1 (average -2).  (e) CH3COOH - BOTH carbons underlined: C of CH3 = -3, C of COOH = +3 (average 0).
reasoning: (a) K = +1 so the I3 unit is -1; 3I = -1 -> I = -1/3. (b) 2(+1) + 4S + 6(-2) = 0 -> 4S = +10 -> S = +2.5. (c) 3Fe + 4(-2) = 0 -> 3Fe = +8 -> Fe = +8/3. The rationalisation for (a)-(c) is exactly the 'Paradox of Fractional Oxidation Number' box on p-10: a fractional value is only an AVERAGE, and the structure shows the element sitting in two different whole-number states. That box names Fe3O4 explicitly as a mixed oxide and gives +5,0,0,+5 for S4O6(2-). (d),(e) are handled the other way - not by averaging but per atom, because each carbon is underlined separately. Bond-by-bond, using 'the electron pair in a covalent bond belongs entirely to the more electronegative element' (p-04/05): a C-H bond gives C -1 each (C 2.55 > H 2.20), a C-O bond gives C +1 each, and a C-C bond gives 0. Ethanol: CH3 carbon has 3 C-H + 1 C-C = -3; CH2OH carbon has 2 C-H (-2) + 1 C-O (+1) + 1 C-C (0) = -1. Cross-check by averaging: C2H6O gives 2C + 6 - 2 = 0 -> average -2 = (-3 + -1)/2. Acetic acid: CH3 carbon = -3; COOH carbon has C=O (+2) + C-O of the OH (+1) + C-C (0) = +3. Cross-check: C2H4O2 gives 2C + 4 - 4 = 0 -> average 0 = (-3 + +3)/2. This is the rationalisation the question asks for: the two carbons in an organic molecule are NOT in the same oxidation state, and only the per-atom (structural) treatment shows it.

answer: (a) CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O: REDOX. Cu +2 -> 0 (reduced); H 0 -> +1 (oxidised); O stays -2.  (b) Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2: REDOX. Fe +3 -> 0 (reduced); C +2 -> +4 (oxidised); O stays -2.  (c) 4BCl3 + 3LiAlH4 -> 2B2H6 + 3LiCl + 3AlCl3: on a consistent electronegativity-based assignment NO element changes oxidation number, so this is NOT a redox reaction - it is a metathesis (hydride-for-chloride exchange). Full assignment - LEFT: BCl3 B = +3, Cl = -1; LiAlH4 Li = +1, Al = +3, H = -1. RIGHT: B2H6 B = +3, H = -1; LiCl Li = +1, Cl = -1; AlCl3 Al = +3, Cl = -1. Every element: B +3 -> +3, Cl -1 -> -1, Li +1 -> +1, Al +3 -> +3, H -1 -> -1.  (d) 2K + F2 -> 2K(+)F(-): REDOX (combination). K 0 -> +1 (oxidised); F 0 -> -1 (reduced).  (e) 4NH3 + 5O2 -> 4NO + 6H2O: REDOX. N -3 -> +2 (oxidised); O 0 -> -2 (reduced); H stays +1.
reasoning: (a),(b),(d),(e) are straightforward and HIGH on their own. The whole of my MED sits on (c). Working for (c): BCl3 - Cl is more electronegative than B so Cl = -1 and B = +3. LiAlH4 - rule 2 on p-05 states outright that 'Aluminium is regarded to have an oxidation number of +3 in all its compounds' and Li = +1, so the four hydrogens must total -4 and H = -1 (hydridic), which is also what the electronegativity principle gives since Al 1.61 < H 2.20. B2H6 - B 2.04 < H 2.20, so hydrogen again takes the bonding pair: H = -1 and B = +3. This is the standard treatment of a boron hydride (the same convention that makes Si +4 in SiH4 and P -3 in PH3). LiCl and AlCl3 are trivial. Nothing moves; the reaction is a double-displacement in which H- and Cl- swap partners, which is also what it is chemically (diborane synthesis from BCl3/LiAlH4 is a hydride metathesis, not an electron transfer). RUNNER-UP, and it wins if you apply rule 4 on p-05 LITERALLY rather than the electronegativity principle it is a shorthand for: rule 4 says H = +1 'except when it is bonded to metals in binary compounds', and boron is not a metal, so H in B2H6 would be +1 and hence B = -3. On that reading (c) IS redox - boron reduced +3 -> -3 (4 B x 6 e = 24 e gained) and hydrogen oxidised -1 -> +1 (12 H x 2 e = 24 e lost), which balances. Note the electron balance is NOT independent evidence for that reading: flipping the sign convention on the same 12 hydrogens must balance by construction, since the LHS is untouched and B2H6 sums to zero either way. What would have to be true for the runner-up to win: that rule 4 governs B2H6 rather than the foundational statement on p-04 that 'the electron pair in a covalent bond belongs entirely to the more electronegative element'. I have taken the foundational principle as governing, because p-05 introduces the numbered rules only as a convenience for when you cannot tell which element is more electronegative - and here you can.

Either the stem over-claims, or the intended answer applies rule 4 literally to B2H6. answer: H2O(s) + F2(g) -> HF(g) + HOF(g) is a redox reaction. OXYGEN is oxidised, from -2 in H2O to 0 in HOF. FLUORINE is reduced, from 0 in F2 to -1 (in both HF and HOF). Hydrogen is +1 throughout and does not change.
reasoning: Left: H2O has H = +1, O = -2; F2 is an element so F = 0. Right: HF has H = +1, F = -1. HOF - fluorine is the most electronegative element, more so than oxygen, so F = -1 here (this is exactly the second exception on p-05, where oxygen bonded to fluorine stops being -2); with H = +1 and F = -1 the sum forces O = 0. So the two fluorine atoms of F2 both go from 0 to -1, gaining 2 electrons between them, while the single oxygen goes from -2 to 0, losing 2 electrons. The electron count balances, confirming the assignment. This is one of the few reactions in which oxygen is the species OXIDISED, which is why the chapter sets it: it shows that 'oxidation' cannot be defined as 'addition of oxygen'.
flag: Worth noting explicitly in a model answer: the fluorine in HOF is -1, NOT positive, and the oxygen is 0. Assigning O = -2 in HOF (the reflex) would force F = +1 and make the question look like it has no oxidised species.

answer: H2SO5: the naive calculation (all O = -2) gives S = +8. Cr2O7(2-): Cr = +6. NO3(-): N = +5. The IMPOSSIBLE one is the sulphur value: +8 cannot occur, because sulphur is a group-16 element whose highest possible oxidation number is group number - 10 = +6. The fallacy is the assumption that every oxygen in H2SO5 is -2. H2SO5 (peroxymonosulphuric acid, Caro's acid) contains a PEROXIDE linkage -O-O-, and those two oxygens are -1 each. Recomputing: 2(+1) + S + 3(-2) + 2(-1) = 0 -> S = +6, which is legitimate. Structures: H2SO5 = HO-S(=O)2-O-O-H, a tetrahedral S carrying two S=O, one -OH and one -O-O-H peroxy arm. Cr2O7(2-) = two CrO4 tetrahedra joined through one bridging oxygen, (O)3Cr-O-Cr(O)3(2-), with every oxygen -2 and no O-O bond, so +6 stands. NO3(-) = trigonal planar nitrogen, a resonance hybrid of one N=O and two N-O(-), all oxygens -2, so +5 stands and equals nitrogen's maximum (group 15 -> 15 - 10 = +5).
reasoning: H2SO5 with all O = -2: 2 + S - 10 = 0 -> S = +8. The p-05 rule 'the highest oxidation number of a representative element is the group number for the first two groups and the group number minus 10 for the other groups' caps S at +6 (the table on p-06 lists SF6 as the group-16 maximum, +6). So +8 is not merely unusual, it is forbidden - which is the flag that an assumption has failed. The only assumption available to fail is the oxygen rule, and p-05 gives the peroxide exception. Cr2O7(2-): 2Cr - 14 = -2 -> Cr = +6; chromium is group 6 so +6 is exactly its maximum - fine. NO3(-): N - 6 = -1 -> N = +5 = 15 - 10 - fine. So only ONE of the three carries a fallacy, and the exercise's phrase 'count for the fallacy' points at H2SO5.
flag: The stem's wording 'Count for the fallacy' is odd English (presumably 'account for the fallacy'). Also note the answer must say the fallacy is in H2SO5 ONLY - Cr(VI) and N(V) are both perfectly legitimate and are there as controls.

answer: (a) Mercury(II) chloride = HgCl2.  (b) Nickel(II) sulphate = NiSO4.  (c) Tin(IV) oxide = SnO2.  (d) Thallium(I) sulphate = Tl2SO4.  (e) Iron(III) sulphate = Fe2(SO4)3.  (f) Chromium(III) oxide = Cr2O3.
reasoning: Stock notation (p-06): the Roman numeral is the oxidation number of the metal. Balance it against Cl = -1, O = -2, SO4 = -2. (a) Hg(+2) + 2Cl(-1) = 0. (b) Ni(+2) + SO4(-2) = 0. (c) Sn(+4) + 2O(-2) = 0. (d) 2Tl(+1) + SO4(-2) = 0 -> Tl2SO4. (e) 2Fe(+3) = +6 needs 3 SO4(-2) = -6 -> Fe2(SO4)3. (f) 2Cr(+3) = +6 needs 3 O(-2) = -6 -> Cr2O3.

answer: (a) 2AgBr + C6H6O2 -> 2Ag + 2HBr + C6H4O2: oxidised = C6H6O2 (hydroquinone, loses 2 H to become quinone); reduced = AgBr (Ag +1 -> 0); oxidising agent = AgBr; reducing agent = C6H6O2.  (b) HCHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]+ + 3OH- -> 2Ag + HCOO- + 4NH3 + 2H2O: oxidised = HCHO (C 0 -> +2); reduced = [Ag(NH3)2]+ (Ag +1 -> 0); oxidising agent = [Ag(NH3)2]+; reducing agent = HCHO.  (c) HCHO + 2Cu(2+) + 5OH- -> Cu2O + HCOO- + 3H2O: oxidised = HCHO (C 0 -> +2); reduced = Cu(2+) (Cu +2 -> +1); oxidising agent = Cu(2+); reducing agent = HCHO.  (d) N2H4 + 2H2O2 -> N2 + 4H2O: oxidised = N2H4 (N -2 -> 0); reduced = H2O2 (O -1 -> -2); oxidising agent = H2O2; reducing agent = N2H4.  (e) Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4 -> 2PbSO4 + 2H2O: oxidised = Pb (metal, 0 -> +2); reduced = PbO2 (Pb +4 -> +2); oxidising agent = PbO2; reducing agent = Pb.
reasoning: Oxidation numbers: (a) Ag is +1 in AgBr and 0 as the metal; hydroquinone C6H6O2 -> quinone C6H4O2 is a loss of two hydrogens, i.e. oxidation. (b),(c) HCHO: 2(+1) for the two H and -2 for O give C = 0; HCOO-: +1 for H and -4 for two O against a total of -1 give C = +2, so carbon is oxidised by 2. Silver in the diammine complex is +1 (both NH3 are neutral ligands) and goes to 0. Copper goes +2 -> +1 in Cu2O. (d) N2H4: 2N + 4(+1) = 0 -> N = -2, going to 0 in N2; peroxide oxygen is -1 (p-05 exception) going to -2 in water. (e) Elemental Pb is 0 and goes to +2 in PbSO4; Pb in PbO2 is +4 and also goes to +2. Both lead atoms converge on the same oxidation state - a comproportionation, the exact reverse of a disproportionation, and the reason this part is set. Note in every part the oxidising agent is the substance REDUCED and the reducing agent is the substance OXIDISED, per the definitions on p-06.

answer: XeO6(4-) + 2F- + 6H+ -> XeO3 + F2 + 3H2O. Xenon is +8 in XeO6(4-) and +6 in XeO3, so Xe is REDUCED (+8 -> +6, gaining 2 electrons). The species OXIDISED is the fluoride ion, F- going from -1 to 0 in F2. The reaction therefore occurs because XeO6(4-) is a strong enough oxidant to oxidise F- to F2. Conclusion about Na4XeO6: it is an extremely powerful oxidising agent - stronger even than fluorine itself, since Table 7.1 puts F2/F- at the top of the series at +2.87 V (the strongest oxidant listed), and anything able to oxidise F- to F2 must sit above it.
reasoning: XeO6(4-): Xe + 6(-2) = -4 -> Xe = +8. XeO3: Xe + 3(-2) = 0 -> Xe = +6. So xenon drops by 2 and cannot be the oxidised species. The only other element changing is fluorine: -1 in F- to 0 in F2, a loss of one electron per atom, 2 electrons for the 2 F-, which exactly matches the 2 electrons xenon gains. Hydrogen (+1) and oxygen (-2) are unchanged. Since F2 is the strongest oxidant in Table 7.1, a reagent that drives F- uphill to F2 must be a stronger oxidant still - that is the inference the question is fishing for.

answer: (a) basic: 2MnO4- + 6I- + 4H2O -> 2MnO2 + 3I2 + 8OH-.  (b) acidic: 2MnO4- + 5SO2 + 2H2O + H+ -> 2Mn(2+) + 5HSO4-.  (c) acidic: H2O2 + 2Fe(2+) + 2H+ -> 2Fe(3+) + 2H2O.  (d) acidic: Cr2O7(2-) + 3SO2 + 2H+ -> 2Cr(3+) + 3SO4(2-) + H2O.
reasoning: (a) Reduction MnO4- (Mn +7) -> MnO2 (Mn +4), 3 e-. In acid: MnO4- + 4H+ + 3e- -> MnO2 + 2H2O; convert to base by adding 4 OH- to both sides and cancelling: MnO4- + 2H2O + 3e- -> MnO2 + 4OH-. Oxidation: 2I- -> I2 + 2e-. Cross-multiply 2 and 3 for 6 electrons and add. Check: Mn 2/2, I 6/6, O 8+4=12 / 4+8=12, H 8/8, charge -8/-8. (b) Reduction MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn(2+) + 4H2O. Oxidation SO2 -> HSO4- (S +4 -> +6): SO2 + 2H2O -> HSO4- + 3H+ + 2e-. Multiply 2 and 5 for 10 electrons, add, then cancel 15 of the 16 H+ and 8 of the 10 H2O. Check: Mn 2/2, S 5/5, O 8+10+2=20 / 20, H 4+1=5 / 5, charge -2+1=-1 / +4-5=-1. (c) Reduction H2O2 + 2H+ + 2e- -> 2H2O (the H2O2/H2O couple, +1.78 V in Table 7.1). Oxidation Fe(2+) -> Fe(3+) + e-, taken twice. Check: charge +4+2=+6 / +6. (d) Reduction Cr2O7(2-) + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr(3+) + 7H2O (Table 7.1, +1.33 V). Oxidation SO2 + 2H2O -> SO4(2-) + 4H+ + 2e-, taken three times. Add and cancel 12 H+ and 6 H2O. Check: Cr 2/2, S 3/3, O 7+6=13 / 12+1=13, H 2/2, charge 0/0.

answer: (a) AS PRINTED (with HPO2-): 5P4 + 12OH- + 12H2O -> 8PH3 + 12HPO2-. This is a DISPROPORTIONATION: phosphorus goes 0 -> -3 in PH3 (reduced) and 0 -> +2 in HPO2- (oxidised), so P4 is BOTH the oxidising agent and the reducing agent.  (b) 3N2H4 + 4ClO3- -> 6NO + 4Cl- + 6H2O. Oxidising agent = ClO3- (Cl +5 -> -1); reducing agent = N2H4 (N -2 -> +2). Note the OH- cancels completely, so no OH- or H+ appears in the final equation.  (c) Cl2O7 + 4H2O2 + 2OH- -> 2ClO2- + 4O2 + 5H2O. Oxidising agent = Cl2O7 (Cl +7 -> +3); reducing agent = H2O2 (peroxide O -1 -> 0).
reasoning: (a) HPO2- as printed: H = +1, two O = -4, total charge -1, so P = +2. PH3: H = +1 (P 2.19 vs H 2.20), so P = -3. Half-reactions in base - reduction P4 + 12H2O + 12e- -> 4PH3 + 12OH-; oxidation P4 + 12OH- -> 4HPO2- + 4H2O + 8e- (charge fixes 12 OH-, then O and H both close). LCM of 12 and 8 is 24, so take reduction x2 and oxidation x3, add, and cancel 24 OH- and 12 H2O. Final check: P 20/20, O 12+12=24 / 24, H 12+24=36 / 24+12=36, charge -12/-12. Electron audit: 8 P reduced x 3 e = 24 gained, 12 P oxidised x 2 e = 24 lost. (b) N2H4 N = -2; NO N = +2, so 4 e per N, 8 e per N2H4. ClO3- Cl = +5 -> Cl- = -1, 6 e. Oxidation N2H4 + 8OH- -> 2NO + 6H2O + 8e-; reduction ClO3- + 3H2O + 6e- -> Cl- + 6OH-. LCM 24: x3 and x4. All 24 OH- cancel. Check: N 6/6, H 12/12, Cl 4/4, O 12 / 6+6=12, charge -4/-4. (c) Cl2O7 Cl = +7; ClO2- Cl = +3, so 4 e per Cl, 8 e per Cl2O7. H2O2 O = -1 -> 0 in O2, 2 e per H2O2. Reduction Cl2O7 + 3H2O + 8e- -> 2ClO2- + 6OH-; oxidation H2O2 + 2OH- -> O2 + 2H2O + 2e-, taken four times. Add, cancel 6 OH- and 3 H2O. Check: Cl 2/2, O 7+8+2=17 / 4+8+5=17, H 8+2=10 / 10, charge -2/-2.

Oxidation half: Mn(3+) -> MnO2 (Mn +3 -> +4), balance O with water and H with H+ in acid: Mn(3+) + 2H2O -> MnO2 + 4H+ + e- (charge +3 left, +4 -1 = +3 right). answer: (a) Only a negative oxidation state: F (fluorine).  (b) Only a positive oxidation state: Cs (caesium).  (c) Both positive and negative oxidation states: I (iodine).  (d) Neither positive nor negative: Ne (neon).
reasoning: (a) Fluorine is the most electronegative element there is, so in every compound it takes the bonding electrons - p-05 rule 5 states flatly 'In all its compounds, fluorine has an oxidation number of -1.' It can never be positive. (b) Caesium is an alkali metal with a single, very loosely held valence electron and the lowest ionisation energy of the four; it only ever loses it, giving +1, and never gains electrons. (c) Iodine is a halogen but a relatively electropositive one - it is -1 as iodide, and positive when bonded to the more electronegative oxygen or fluorine, which p-05 rule 5 says explicitly ('Chlorine, bromine and iodine when combined with oxygen ... have positive oxidation numbers'), giving +1, +3, +5, +7 in the oxoacids and oxoanions. (d) Neon is a noble gas with a closed octet; it forms no compounds at all, so it is 0 and nothing else. (Xenon and krypton do form compounds - hence the exercise picks neon, not any noble gas.)

answer: Cl2 + SO2 + 2H2O -> 2HCl + H2SO4  (equivalently, in ionic form: Cl2 + SO2 + 2H2O -> 2Cl- + SO4(2-) + 4H+). Chlorine is reduced (0 -> -1) and sulphur is oxidised (+4 -> +6), so SO2 is the reducing agent that destroys the excess chlorine.
reasoning: Half reactions in water: Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl- (Table 7.1, +1.36 V) and SO2 + 2H2O -> SO4(2-) + 4H+ + 2e-. Two electrons each way, so they add 1:1. Molecular check on Cl2 + SO2 + 2H2O -> 2HCl + H2SO4: Cl 2/2, S 1/1, O 2+2 = 4 / 4, H 4 / 2+2 = 4. Feasibility check from Table 7.1 - the Cl2/Cl- couple sits well above any sulphate/SO2 couple, so chlorine is comfortably strong enough to take SO2 up to sulphate, which is why this is the standard dechlorination treatment. Both products stay in solution as dilute acids, which is the point for drinking water.

answer: 15.00 g of nitric oxide. Oxygen is the LIMITING reagent; ammonia is in excess.
reasoning: The first step of the Ostwald process is 4NH3(g) + 5O2(g) -> 4NO(g) + 6H2O(g) (the same equation as Ex 7.3(e)). Moles available: M(NH3) = 14 + 3(1) = 17 g/mol, so n(NH3) = 10.00 / 17 = 0.5882 mol. M(O2) = 2(16) = 32 g/mol, so n(O2) = 20.00 / 32 = 0.6250 mol. Which runs out first: 0.5882 mol NH3 would require 0.5882 x (5/4) = 0.7353 mol O2, but only 0.6250 mol is present, so oxygen is limiting. Checking the other way round, 0.6250 mol O2 consumes 0.6250 x (4/5) = 0.5000 mol NH3, leaving 0.5882 - 0.5000 = 0.0882 mol NH3 (about 1.5 g) unreacted - consistent. Product: NO forms in a 4:5 ratio with O2, so n(NO) = 0.6250 x (4/5) = 0.5000 mol. M(NO) = 14 + 16 = 30 g/mol. Mass = 0.5000 x 30 = 15.00 g. The word 'maximum' in the stem is the signal that this is a limiting-reagent question and that 100% conversion is to be assumed.
flag: An answer of about 17.6 g would come from wrongly taking NH3 as limiting (0.5882 mol NH3 -> 0.5882 mol NO x 30 = 17.65 g). That is the trap the numbers are chosen to set, so 15.00 g vs 17.65 g is the discriminating comparison if the two passes disagree.

answer: (a) Fe(3+) and I- : FEASIBLE. E(Fe3+/Fe2+) = +0.77 V, E(I2/I-) = +0.54 V; Ecell = 0.77 - 0.54 = +0.23 V. Reaction: 2Fe(3+) + 2I- -> 2Fe(2+) + I2.  (b) Ag+ and Cu(s): FEASIBLE. E(Ag+/Ag) = +0.80 V, E(Cu2+/Cu) = +0.34 V; Ecell = 0.80 - 0.34 = +0.46 V. Reaction: 2Ag+ + Cu -> 2Ag + Cu(2+).  (c) Fe(3+) and Cu(s): FEASIBLE.
